title: Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services
summary: This sub-technique covers registering ordinary third-party web services, such as code repositories, cloud storage, paste sites, or social platforms, and using them as operational infrastructure. Unlike buying a server or a domain, the operator never owns the hosting, so the traffic destination is a legitimate, widely used provider that most organisations already permit. That makes the activity valuable for phishing lures hosted on trusted links, for command and control where the implant polls a public application programming interface, and for exfiltration over web services. The parent technique covers acquisition broadly; here the acquired asset is an account and its hosted content. The defender's problem is that the network path is legitimate, so detection shifts to account behaviour: accounts created recently, service access by processes that should never use a browser, unusual volumes of uploads or downloads to a single consumer account, and notification from the provider itself when abuse is discovered.

beginner.definition: Web services are free or cheap online tools such as code hosts, cloud drives, and social sites. This sub-technique is about an attacker creating accounts on those services to use later. The parent technique covers getting infrastructure in general. Here the asset is an account on someone else's platform.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your firewall already allows these services, because staff use them every day. A malicious file on a popular code host looks like an ordinary download. When attackers hide inside trusted platforms, blocking the whole service usually costs the business more than it saves, so detection has to be smarter.
howItWorks: The attacker registers an account on a popular service using a disposable email address.
They upload bait files, fake forms, or a page that looks official.
They send links from that trusted service to targets, so filters see a known good domain.
Malware may also call the service's programming interface to receive commands or return data.
Traffic blends with normal staff use because it shares addresses and certificates with everyone.
When notice arrives, the attacker abandons the account and opens another within minutes.
beginner.example: Imagine a public notice board in a station where anyone may pin a card. A con artist pins a card with a polished advert. Travellers trust the board, so they trust the card. Station staff see only that a card was pinned, not who pinned it or what the small print really offers.
takeaways: Trust in a platform does not transfer to every file or account hosted there.
Look at which process or user talks to a service, not only at the destination.
Data volume to one consumer account is a strong signal of hidden exfiltration.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent Acquire Infrastructure technique.
Describe how legitimate web services are abused for delivery, control, and exfiltration.
Identify log sources that record access to web services from your environment.
Distinguish normal staff use of a service from suspicious account or volume behaviour.
Describe how provider abuse reporting supports defensive response.
